unit.title: Clean and maintain soft floor and furnishings

summary: This unit teaches you to clean and care for carpets, rugs, upholstery and curtains in a villa, guest house or hotel: check the fibre and the label, vacuum properly, remove stains, deep clean by the right method, dry the work quickly in Jamaica's climate, and keep soft furnishings looking good for longer. You will also learn to use equipment and chemicals safely.

blocks.p: Carpets, rugs, curtains, cushions and sofas make a guest room feel warm and comfortable, but they also hold dust, sand, spills and germs. They are expensive to replace and easy to ruin with the wrong product or too much water. A trained worker can keep them clean for years. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

**Soft floors and furnishings** means carpets, rugs, curtains and sheers, cushions and upholstered chairs and sofas. The unit's main idea is simple: **find out what the item is made of, use the gentlest method that works, and dry it fast.**

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre. In the practical tasks you vacuum a carpet, remove stains and deep clean a rug and an upholstered chair. The assessor watches your checks, safety, stain method and drying, as well as the result.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Photograph the item, the stain and the stages of work. Do not photograph any guest's belongings or room numbers.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Electrical machines and water
Electric shock; a ruined motor
Never use an ordinary dry vacuum on water: only a wet and dry machine
Keep plugs and sockets dry; plug in with dry hands
Check plugs and cables before every use and do not use a damaged one
Cables
Trips and falls; cut cables
Keep the cable behind you and to one side, out of walkways
Never pull the machine by its cable
Pull the plug, not the cable, to unplug
Chemicals: stain removers, shampoos, solvents
Skin and eye burns; fumes; fire
Read the label and the SDS
Wear gloves and eye protection
Air the room
Never mix products, especially bleach with others
Keep solvents away from flames and sparks
Wet floors
Slips
Put up wet floor signs
Keep the area closed until dry
Heavy machines and wet rugs
Back strain
Use a trolley and bend your knees
Get help to carry a wet rug or roll it
Empty tanks before lifting an extraction machine
Noise and dust
Hearing and breathing problems
Use a vacuum with a good filter; wear a dust mask if the dust is heavy
Needles, glass and coins in carpet
Cuts and pricks; damaged machine
Look before you vacuum; pick them up with care and report valuables

blocks.note: If a vacuum cleaner smells of burning, makes a strange noise or throws sparks, **switch it off, unplug it, label it faulty and report it**. Do not carry on, and never pour water into it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica uses 110 V (and 220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. A damp carpet, a hot, humid room and an extension cord on the floor are a bad mix. Keep extension cords short, dry and away from wet areas.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **PPE** means personal protective equipment. For soft-floor cleaning it usually means gloves, closed non-slip shoes and, for chemicals and sprays, eye protection. Wear a dust mask for very dusty work. Check what the label and the SDS say.

ul: Clean when the room is empty, and, for deep cleaning, when it will not be needed for some hours.
Pick up hairpins, coins and earrings before you vacuum: they can damage the machine and may belong to a guest. Record valuables and hand them in as the rules say.
Put out signs and close the area while it is wet.
The **pile** is the yarn that stands up from the **backing**. Pile can be **cut** (the loops are cut, making soft ends) or **loop** (uncut loops, which are hard-wearing and harder to snag if tight).
The fibre, the pile height and the density decide how the carpet wears and how it should be cleaned.
Dirt and grit settle between the fibres. When people walk on it, grit cuts the fibres like tiny blades. That is why vacuuming is the most important job.

head: Fibre
Where you find it
Care points
rows: Wool
Good carpets and rugs
Springy and hard-wearing but expensive. Hot water, strong alkalis and bleach damage it. It can shrink and its dye can bleed. Moths and carpet beetles eat it.
Nylon
Many hotel carpets
Strong, wears well and cleans well; check dye fastness in sunlight.
Polyester
Some carpets, curtains and cushions
Soft and resists stains; can hold oily marks.
Polypropylene (olefin)
Some contract carpets and outdoor mats
Resists water and many stains but holds oil; can crush.
Cotton
Rugs, curtains, cushion covers
Can shrink; colours may run.
Viscose / rayon
Some rugs and curtains
Weak when wet and can mark easily; take great care and follow the label.
Blends
Many fabrics
Clean by the most delicate fibre in the blend.

blocks.h: Care labels and sofa cleaning codes

blocks.p: Always look for a **care label** or the maker's instructions on a rug, cushion, curtain or sofa. Many upholstered items carry a **cleaning code**.

head: Code
What it means
How to clean it
rows: W
Water-based cleaner
Use a water-based product or a foam shampoo. Do not soak it.
S
Solvent (dry-cleaning) product only
Use a dry-cleaning solvent and no water. Do it in an aired room, away from flames.
W/S or S/W
Either water-based or solvent
Choose the gentler method and test first.
X
Vacuum or brush only
Use **no liquid cleaner at all**. Send it to a specialist for anything more.

blocks.note: If there is **no label**, treat the item as delicate: vacuum, test a hidden spot with the mildest cleaner and ask your supervisor before using water or solvent.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Machine or tool
What it is for
rows: Upright vacuum
Stands upright; has a turning brush roll in its head. Good for large carpeted areas.
Cylinder (canister) vacuum
A tank pulled along on wheels with a hose. Good for stairs, furniture and hard floors.
Backpack vacuum
Worn on the back. Lets a cleaner work quickly in large rooms and on stairs.
Wet and dry vacuum
The only type that can safely pick up water as well as dust.
Floor head
Wide head for open floor and carpet; a brush roll helps lift pile.
Crevice tool
Long, narrow nozzle for edges, corners and along skirting boards.
Upholstery tool
Small, wide nozzle for sofas, chairs and cushions.
Dusting brush
Round, soft brush for curtains, lampshades and ornaments.

ul: The plug and cable are undamaged, and the cable is not twisted or cut.
The bag or dust container is not full: a full bag lowers suction. Empty it or change the bag.
The filter is clean as the maker says. A blocked filter lowers suction and can overheat the motor.
The brush roll turns freely and is free of hair and thread. The hose is not blocked.
The right head or tool is fitted for the job.

blocks.p: Vacuuming removes the grit that wears carpet. Done regularly and well, it is the best way to make carpets last. Do it **before** any stain removal or deep cleaning, because wet dirt turns to mud.

flow: Check the room and pick up small items, rubbish and valuables
Move light furniture; look under beds and chairs
Check the machine, the plug and the bag
Plug in at the socket nearest the far end of the room and work back towards it, keeping the cable behind you
Vacuum the edges and corners with the crevice tool
Vacuum the main area in slow, overlapping strokes, forwards and backwards
Vacuum under furniture and replace it exactly where it was
Check the finished area for even stroke lines and no grit in corners
Empty the bag as needed and put the machine away

ul: **Slow, overlapping strokes** pick up more than fast ones, because the machine needs time to draw the dirt out.
Do not push hard on the handle. It does not dig out more dust, and it makes the machine hard to push.
Do the most-used areas, such as doorways, corridors and in front of chairs, more often and for longer. These wear fastest.
Vacuum **both ways** across the pile on the heavily soiled areas.
Keep the cable behind you and to one side, out of walkways, and never pull the machine by its cable.

head: Item
How to vacuum it
rows: Edges and skirting boards
Crevice tool, slowly.
Upholstered chairs and sofa cushions
Upholstery tool: both sides of the cushions, and the gaps along the seat and arms. Lift the cushions.
Rugs with a fringe
Keep the brush roll **off the fringe**, or it will wind up and tear. Brush the fringe straight by hand afterwards.
Curtains
Soft brush tool on low suction, from the top down. Do not pull the fabric.
Stairs
Hose and tool, working from the top step down, so that dust falls onto the steps below.
Delicate or antique rugs
Low suction, no brush roll; or follow the maker's or owner's instructions.

blocks.note: In a villa, sand is the biggest enemy of carpets. It is sharp and cuts the fibres. Put **mats at the doors**, clean them often and vacuum the areas near the entrance every day.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Most stains come out if you act **fast** and use the right method. A stain that has dried, or been rubbed, or been treated with the wrong product can become permanent. Follow the same steps every time.

flow: Act at once and wear gloves
Scrape up any solid with a spoon or blunt knife
Blot the liquid with a clean, dry, white cloth or paper towel, pressing down, never rubbing
Test the remover on a hidden spot
Apply a little remover to the cloth, not to the carpet, and dab from the outside edge of the stain towards the middle
Blot, using a clean part of the cloth each time
Rinse lightly with cold water and blot dry
Check the stain is gone; if not, repeat or report
Let the spot dry, then vacuum or brush the pile

ul: **Blot, do not rub.** Rubbing spreads the stain and damages the fibres.
Work **from the outside edge towards the middle** so the stain does not spread.
Use a **white cloth**, so no dye comes off onto the carpet.
**Test** any stain remover on a hidden part first: it may bleach, damage or fade the fabric.
Do not over-wet. Too much liquid soaks into the backing and makes the stain come back as it dries (this is called **wicking**).
Never use bleach on carpet, and never mix chemicals.
If you cannot remove a stain, **report it** so a specialist or a deep clean can be arranged. Do not cover it up, keep adding more remover or cut the carpet.

head: Stain
What to do
rows: Coffee, tea, fruit juice, sorrel, wine and rum punch
Blot quickly. Dab with cold water and a little mild detergent, then blot. Use a spotter for what remains. Test first. Do not use hot water.
Blood (wear gloves)
Use **cold** water, never hot: heat sets the stain. Blot; use a mild detergent if needed. Follow the property's rules for body fluids.
Grease, oil, sunscreen, make-up
Blot, then use a grease spotter (solvent-based) that suits the fabric's label, working from the outside in. Do not use water only: oil does not mix with it.
Chewing gum

Harden it with ice in a bag or a freezing spray, then lift or break it off. Remove the last of it with a dry-cleaning solvent if the label allows. Never pull it while it is soft, never use hot water and never cut the carpet.
Mud
Let it dry, then brush and vacuum it. Treat what is left as a stain.
Ink
Blot, then use a spotter made for ink. Test first, and work from the outside in.
Candle wax
Let it harden, scrape off, then cover with blotting paper and press with a warm iron to lift the rest; then treat any colour left.
Pet or vomit stains
Scrape up; blot; clean and disinfect as the rules say; use a deodoriser; wear gloves.

blocks.note: Use **cold** water on protein stains, such as blood, egg, milk and vomit. Heat cooks protein into the fibres and sets it for good.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A **cigarette burn** cannot be cleaned out. **Report it**: it may need a repair or a charge. Do not rub in ash, move a chair over it or cut out the fibres.
A **pulled thread or loop** is snipped level, not pulled.
A **spreading dark patch** after drying (wicking) means too much liquid was used; report it.

blocks.p: Vacuuming takes out dry dirt. **Deep cleaning** removes the greasy film and ground-in dirt that vacuuming cannot. A hotel carpet is deep cleaned as the schedule says, for example every few months, and sooner for soiled areas. Choose the method by the fibre, the label, the soil and how soon the room is needed.

head: Method
How it works
Good for
Take care
rows: Hot water extraction (often called steam cleaning)
The machine sprays hot cleaning solution into the pile and sucks it back out, with the dirt.
A deep clean of heavily soiled carpet; the most thorough.
Can over-wet; needs time to dry; check the fibre and dye first.
Bonnet cleaning
A rotary machine spins an absorbent pad (a bonnet) damped with solution over the surface, and the pad takes up the dirt. Change or rinse the pad often.
Regular, quick maintenance of the top of the carpet; low moisture.
Cleans the surface only; can push dirt down if the pad is dirty.
Dry compound
A damp absorbent powder is brushed into the carpet and later vacuumed up, with the dirt.
Where the room must be used again soon; little water.
Must all be vacuumed up; dust can be a problem.
Shampooing (foam)
A foam is worked in and vacuumed or extracted later.
Old method for general cleaning.
Residue left behind attracts dirt.

blocks.h: Hot water extraction step by step

flow: Read the label and the SDS and choose the correct solution
Clear and move the furniture; put tabs or foil under the legs of furniture that cannot be moved
Vacuum the carpet very well
Spot-treat stains first
Test the solution and the colour-fastness on a hidden part
Pre-spray the traffic areas if the method needs it, and leave for the time on the label
Fill the machine's solution tank to the mark, with solution mixed as the label says
Clean in straight, overlapping rows, spraying on the push and sucking back on the pull, working back towards the door
Make a final dry pass to remove as much water as you can
Groom the pile with a carpet rake or brush so it dries evenly
Air and dry the carpet; keep the area closed
Empty and rinse the tanks, clean the nozzle and hoses, and store the machine

ul: **Do not over-wet.** Too much water can shrink the carpet, make it smell, grow mould, soak into the backing or bring up stains from below.
Mix solution exactly as the label says. Too strong leaves a sticky residue that attracts dirt.
Move the machine steadily. Stopping in one place soaks the carpet.
Check the label: many wool and hand-made rugs must be cleaned by a specialist.
Test for colour bleeding with a damp white cloth on a hidden corner.
Take the rug outside, if the rules allow, and beat or vacuum both sides. Clean it flat. Turn it and clean the back.
Dry flat, off the ground if possible, in the shade. Strong sun fades colours.
Empty and rinse the tanks, clean the nozzle and wipe the machine. Leaving dirty water in a machine makes it smell and breed bacteria.
Record what was cleaned, the method used and any stain that remains.

blocks.p: A damp carpet is a problem. In Jamaica's warm, humid air, **mould and mildew grow fast** on wet carpet and cause a musty smell, health problems and ruined carpet. Dry it as quickly as you can.

flow: Do a final dry extraction pass to remove all the water you can
Open the windows and doors if the air outside is dry, or run the air conditioner or a dehumidifier
Set fans to blow across the surface
Keep traffic off until dry
Check dampness by pressing a clean white cloth on the carpet; it should come up dry
Rake the pile once it is nearly dry

ul: Drying time depends on the method, the carpet, the weather and the air flow; it can be a few hours. Do not shut the room tightly with the heat inside.
Do not walk on the carpet to press out water.
Do not lay old towels or newspaper on a wet carpet: dye or ink can come off onto it.
Do not put furniture back on a damp carpet. **Wood stain and rust from metal feet can mark a wet carpet.** Wait until it is dry or put foil or plastic tabs under the legs.

blocks.note: After heavy rain or flooding, treat wet carpet as an emergency. Report it, as it may need to be lifted and dried or thrown away, because mould can start within a day or two in warm, damp weather.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Check
Standard
rows: Colour and appearance
Even, with no marks left; the pile is lifted and the stroke lines even
Smell
Fresh, with no musty or chemical smell
Dryness
Dry to the touch, or the area still closed off with a sign
Furniture
Back in the correct places and not on damp carpet
Edges and corners
Clean and free of grit
Stains
Gone, or reported

ul: **Vacuum** with the upholstery tool every week, or as the schedule says. Do both sides of cushions, the seat, arms, back and the gaps. Lift the cushions and look for coins, hair and food.
**Turn and plump** the seat and back cushions, so they wear evenly and keep their shape.
**Wipe up spills at once.** Blot; never rub.
Keep sofas out of strong sun, which fades the fabric. Close the curtains or blinds in the hottest part of the day if you can.

blocks.h: Cleaning an upholstered chair or sofa

flow: Read the care label and find the cleaning code
Vacuum the whole item
Test the cleaner on a hidden part
Clean as the code allows: water-based product or foam for W, solvent for S, brush or vacuum only for X
Use as little liquid as possible, working in small sections
Blot, then brush the pile or nap in the same direction
Let it dry fully, with fans, before anyone sits
Replace cushions and check the result

ul: If the code is **X**, use **no liquid**. Vacuum and brush it, and ask a specialist for anything more.
A removable cover with a zip may be washed **only if the care label says so**: many shrink or lose their shape.
Do not soak the filling: wet foam takes a very long time to dry and can grow mould.

head: Problem
What to do
rows: Oily sunscreen stain
Grease spotter that suits the fabric's code, tested first
Shiny, flattened patches on arms
Brush the pile gently; report if it will not lift
Stain you cannot remove
Report it; arrange a specialist clean
Burn or tear
Report it; do not try to hide it
Musty smell
Check for damp; vacuum; air it; report mould

sections.title: Curtains, rugs and keeping soft furnishings looking good

ul: **Sheers** are thin, see-through curtains that let light in and give privacy. **Drapes** are the heavier curtains. Both hang from a **curtain rail** or rod on hooks or rings.
Between deep cleans, **vacuum curtains gently** with the soft brush tool and low suction, from the top down.
Never shake them out of the window each morning, spray them with water or keep them closed day and night.
Spot-clean small marks as for upholstery, testing first.
Dust and sun fade and weaken curtains. Strong Jamaican sunlight **breaks down the dyes** in the cloth, which is why curtains and furnishings in sunny rooms fade.

flow: Read the care label: wash, dry clean or vacuum only
Check the rail, hooks and brackets are sound
Use a safe step stool, with a second person to hold it
Unhook the curtain from one end, lifting it down and folding it as you go
Remove the hooks and note any damage
Clean as the label says
Dry fully; iron or press as the label allows
Re-hang by working from the centre, spacing the hooks evenly
Check the curtains hang straight and the rail runs freely

blocks.note: Never stand on a chair or a table to reach a curtain rail. Use a stable step stool, with someone to hold it. Switch off lights and move cables away first.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Making soft floors and furnishings last

head: Action
Why it helps
rows: Put mats at all doors and clean them often
Stops sand and dirt being walked onto the carpet.
Vacuum regularly and thoroughly
Removes the grit that cuts and wears fibres.
Deal with spills at once
Stops stains setting.
Turn rugs round now and then
They wear and fade evenly.
Move heavy furniture a little from time to time
Stops permanent dents in the pile.
Keep curtains and furniture out of direct sun when possible
Stops colours fading.
Keep rooms dry and aired; use fans and dehumidifiers if needed
Stops mould and mildew.
Deep clean on a regular schedule
Removes the greasy film that attracts dirt.
Check for signs of pests and report them
Catches problems early.

blocks.p: **Moths** and **carpet beetles** eat wool. Their tiny larvae (grubs) make small holes in wool rugs and carpets, often under furniture where it is dark and still. If you see small holes in a wool rug, and tiny grubs or cast skins, report it to your supervisor. Regular vacuuming under furniture helps prevent it. Pest control is done by the property.

ul: Report cigarette burns, tears, unremovable stains, mould, moths, damaged rails and faulty machines.
Record work done, products used and anything left to follow up.
I can name the soft floors and furnishings and say why each needs care.
I can work safely with vacuums, extraction machines and chemicals.
I can check the plug, cable, bag and filter before I vacuum.
I can name common carpet fibres and their care points.
I can read a care label and the cleaning codes W, S, W/S and X.
I can vacuum in slow overlapping strokes and use the right tool for edges, upholstery and fringes.
I can follow the stain steps: act fast, scrape, blot, test, work outside in, rinse and dry.
I can choose the right method for coffee, blood, grease and gum.
I can explain why blood needs cold water and why wicking happens.
I can describe hot water extraction, bonnet and dry compound methods and when to use each.
I can avoid over-wetting a carpet and explain why.
I can dry a carpet quickly and protect it from furniture while damp.
I can clean and care for an upholstered chair or sofa using its code.
I can vacuum, take down and re-hang curtains safely.
I can make carpets last with mats, rotation and regular cleaning, and report burns, mould and moths.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I blot, not rub, because rubbing spreads the stain and damages the fibres.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Carpets, rugs, curtains, cushions and upholstered furniture.
The fibres that stand up from a carpet's backing.
The base that holds the pile of a carpet.
The padding, springs and fabric cover of chairs and sofas.
The rod or track curtains hang from.
Letters on a sofa label (W, S, W/S, X) that show how to clean it.
Pressing a clean cloth on a stain to soak up liquid, without rubbing.
A stain rising back up from the backing as an over-wet carpet dries.
Colour running into water or onto other fabric.
Cleaning that sprays hot solution into carpet and sucks it back out.
An absorbent pad spun on a rotary machine to lift surface dirt.
Damp absorbent powder brushed into carpet and vacuumed up.
A vacuum with a turning brush roll in its head.
A vacuum that can safely pick up water.
A narrow nozzle for edges and corners.
A fungus that grows on damp carpet and fabric.
An insect whose larvae eat wool.

c1.title: Vacuuming a Treasure Beach villa
c1.text: Trainee Kimberly has to vacuum the lounge of a villa in Treasure Beach before new guests arrive at 2 p.m. The carpet has sand near the patio door, and a wool rug with a fringe lies in front of the sofa. Her upright vacuum has a cable with a cut in the outer covering and a bag that is almost full. She finds two hairpins and a small gold earring on the carpet.

c2.title: A sorrel spill in a Kingston lounge
c2.text: A guest at a Kingston guest house spills a glass of sorrel onto a pale beige nylon carpet in the lounge. Trainee Delroy comes within a minute. He has a white cloth, a bottle of mild spotter, a spoon and a bucket of water. Later, after the carpet dries, a brownish patch appears at the same spot.

c3.title: Deep cleaning a lounge in Mandeville
c3.text: A Mandeville guest house wants its lounge carpet deep cleaned this afternoon. The room is booked again at 7 p.m. The carpet is a nylon blend that is grey and dull near the door. Trainee Marcia has a hot water extraction machine, and the lounge is furnished with a wooden coffee table and two metal-legged chairs.

c4.title: Sofa and cushions in a Negril villa
c4.text: In a Negril villa, trainee Jerome has to clean a pale sofa with a care label showing the code W, and an armchair whose label shows the code X. The sofa has an oily sunscreen mark on one arm and the cushion covers have zips with no washing instructions. The villa has just been through humid weather.

c5.title: Curtains and rugs in Falmouth
c5.text: A hotel in Falmouth has curtains that are faded on the sunny side of the room, and sheers that are grey with dust. A wool rug in the corridor has small holes under a cupboard, and trainee Shelly sees tiny grubs there. She has to take down the curtains to clean them.

c6.title: A wet rug and a machine in Port Maria
c6.text: After an extraction clean at a Port Maria property, trainee Anthony wants to carry a heavy, wet rug outside to dry. The extraction machine's water tanks are full of dirty water, and its cable lies across a wet part of the floor. He is working alone, and the weather is humid.

questions.q: What should Kimberly do about the vacuum cleaner before she starts?
o: Wrap tape round the cut and use it quickly
Use it, but keep her feet away from the cut
Report it and take a machine with a good cable
Empty the bag and use the cable as it is
questions.why: A cut cable is an electric shock and fire risk. Do not use it; report it and take a safe machine. A full bag also lowers suction and should be emptied.

questions.q: What should she do about the hairpins and the gold earring?
o: Vacuum them up, as the bag will catch them
Pick them up and hand in the earring, with a record
Leave them on the carpet for the guest to find
Put them in her pocket to keep them safe
questions.why: Small items can damage the vacuum, and the earring may belong to a guest. Pick them up, record any valuables and hand them in; never keep them.

questions.q: How should she vacuum the fringe of the wool rug?
o: Keep the brush roll off the fringe and brush it straight by hand
Run the brush roll across the fringe to straighten it
Pull the fringe straight and vacuum it hard
Trim the fringe so that it cannot get caught
questions.why: A turning brush roll winds up fringes and tears them. Use a tool or lift the head clear, and straighten the fringe by hand.

questions.q: What should Delroy do first?
o: Blot up as much sorrel as he can with the white cloth
Pour a bucket of water over the spill to wash it out
Rub the spill hard with the cloth to work it loose
Leave it to dry and brush it out later
questions.why: Fresh liquid is best removed by blotting before it sinks in. Rubbing spreads the stain and a flood of water pushes it into the backing.

questions.q: Where should Delroy start dabbing the spotter?
o: On the middle of the stain and then out to the clean carpet
In large circles over the whole of the carpet
On the outer edge of the stain, working in towards the middle
Along the pile with a hard brush
questions.why: Working from the outside in stops the stain being pushed outwards into clean carpet. Use a little remover on the cloth and a clean part of the cloth each time.

questions.q: What most likely caused the brown patch to appear after the carpet dried?
o: The spotter is brown and has dried on the surface
The beige nylon changes colour in daylight
The sorrel was not a strong stain and has simply faded
Too much water carried the stain down and it rose again as it dried
questions.why: This is wicking: over-wetting pushes the stain into the backing, and it rises to the surface as the carpet dries. Use as little liquid as possible, and report a stain that returns.

questions.q: Before using the new spotter on the carpet, what should Delroy do?
o: Mix it with bleach to make it stronger
Test it on a hidden part of the carpet
Soak the whole stained area in it for an hour
Ask the guest whether she likes the smell
questions.why: Test every remover on a hidden spot to check it does not fade or damage the fabric. Never mix products.

questions.q: Which method best fits Marcia's job, with the room booked again at 7 p.m.?
o: Hot water extraction, then a dry pass and fans
Soaking the carpet in water, then walking on it to press it out
Shampooing with plenty of foam and leaving the residue in the pile
Spraying the whole carpet and shutting the room tight
questions.why: Extraction cleans deeply and, with a final dry pass and good air flow, can dry in time. Heavy soaking, leftover residue and a shut room all cause problems.

questions.q: What must Marcia do before she starts the machine?
o: Spray the carpet with a bucket of hot water
Put plastic over the carpet to keep the heat in
Move the furniture, and vacuum the carpet well
Add extra solution to the tank to clean better
questions.why: The carpet is cleared and vacuumed first, because wet dirt turns to mud and furniture is in the way. Solution must be mixed as the label says.

questions.q: What should Marcia do about the metal-legged chairs and the wooden table once the carpet is clean?
o: Put them back at once, to have the room ready on time
Put them back after standing on the carpet to press the water out
Put them back with towels under the legs
Wait until it is dry, or use foil tabs under the legs
questions.why: Rust and wood stain can mark a wet carpet. Wait until it is dry or use tabs under the legs.

questions.q: What is the best way to speed up drying?
o: Close all the doors and windows to keep the heat in
Use fans and air conditioning, and keep people off it
Cover it with old newspapers
Walk on it often to press out water
questions.why: Moving air removes moisture, and cooled air from air conditioning is drier. Newspaper can stain it and walking presses dirt in.

questions.q: What should Jerome do about the armchair with the code X?
o: Shampoo it with a little water, as it is a small chair
Clean it with a solvent rubbed in hard
Spray it with the water-based cleaner and rub it dry
Vacuum or brush it only, using no liquid cleaner
questions.why: X means vacuum or brush only; any liquid can damage the fabric. A specialist can be asked about anything more.

questions.q: What kind of product should Jerome use on the oily sunscreen mark on the W sofa?
o: Plain cold water only, because oil mixes well with water
A grease spotter for that fabric, tested first
Bleach, to lift the colour out of the cloth
Furniture polish, rubbed well into the arm
questions.why: Oil needs a grease remover, and it must suit the fabric's code, so test it first. Water alone will not lift oil, and bleach and polish damage the fabric.

questions.q: Should Jerome take the zipped cushion covers off and wash them?
o: Only if the care label says they can be washed
Yes, always: a zip means they are made to be washed
Yes, in hot water, to kill any germs
No, only the guests may wash cushion covers
questions.why: Covers can shrink or change shape. Wash them only if the label allows, otherwise clean them as the code says.

questions.q: Why are the curtains faded on the sunny side?
o: Cold air from the air conditioner bleaches them
They were washed with too little detergent
Strong sunlight breaks down the dyes in the cloth
Sea breezes blow the colour out of the fabric
questions.why: Ultraviolet light breaks down dyes, so curtains and furnishings in sunny rooms fade. Closing blinds in the hottest hours helps.

questions.q: What should Shelly do about the holes and grubs in the wool rug?
o: Wash the rug in hot water, to kill the grubs
Report it, as they are probably moths or carpet beetles
Cover the holes with a patch of tape and carry on
Burn off the grubs with a candle flame
questions.why: Wool is eaten by moth and carpet beetle larvae. Report it so pest control can be arranged; hot water would also shrink the wool.

questions.q: How should Shelly deal with the dusty sheers between deep cleans?
o: Shake them hard out of the window each morning
Spray them with water and leave them to dry
Keep them closed all day and night
Vacuum them gently with the soft brush tool on low suction
questions.why: Gentle vacuuming from the top down removes dust without damaging the cloth. Shaking and spraying damage sheers or leave marks.

questions.q: What is the safest way for Anthony to move the wet rug?
o: Fold it over his shoulder and carry it quickly
Get help, or roll it onto a trolley
Drag it by one corner
Leave it in a heap to drain
questions.why: A wet rug is very heavy and can injure your back. Roll it, use a trolley or get help; dragging damages it.

questions.q: What is wrong with the extraction machine's cable lying across the wet floor?
o: It could cause an electric shock or a trip
It will make the machine run slowly
It will make the cable too dirty to use again
It will stop the solution from flowing
questions.why: Electrical cable and water are a dangerous mix. Keep cables dry, short and out of walkways, and check them before use.

questions.q: What should Anthony do with the extraction machine's tanks and nozzle after the job?
o: Leave the dirty water in for the next job
Wipe the outside only, as the inside cleans itself
Empty and rinse the tanks, and clean the nozzle
Store it with the solution tank full and closed
questions.why: Dirty water left in a machine smells and breeds bacteria. Empty and rinse the tanks, clean the nozzle and hoses and store it clean and dry.
